Text 1
Because knowledge of Linear B script, the writing system of ancient Mycenaean Greece, was lost after the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE, scholars long debated how meaning was represented in its symbols. While many researchers had assumed that the symbols represented concepts or entire words, archaeologist Maria Petros argued in 2015 that they represented much more specific linguistic elements: individual phonemes, the smallest units of sound in spoken language.

Text 2
Current scholarship on Linear B script suggests that its symbols operated with greater complexity than previously understood. Most symbols appear to have represented syllables rather than individual phonemes, though some could function as word-signs for frequently used terms like numbers or titles. For instance, a symbol might represent the syllable "ka" in most contexts but signify the complete word "kanax" (king) when appearing in royal administrative records. Mycenaean scribes thus had to interpret symbol function based on documentary context and content.
